title: Deck Stain Calculator: How Many Gallons?
description: Find gallons of deck stain by deck size, wood condition and coats, using real label coverage for smooth and rough wood, plus a worked example.

cover.alt: A deck with freshly stained boards beside bare boards, a can of stain and a stain roller

tool.name: Deck stain calculator
tool.short: Gallons for one or two coats

keywords: how much deck stain do I need
gallons of stain for a deck
takeaways: Behr lists its semi-transparent stain at 250 to 300 sq ft per gallon for the first coat and 500 to 600 sq ft per gallon for the second coat.
Rough wood drinks far more stain than smooth wood, at 100 to 200 sq ft per gallon for Cabot semi-transparent stain versus 250 to 350 sq ft on smooth wood.
Add up the gallons for each coat on its own, then round the total up to whole gallons before you buy.
body:
For a typical deck in good shape, plan on 1 gallon for every 250 to 300 sq ft on the first coat, and far less on the second coat. A 16 x 20 ft deck (320 sq ft) needs about 2 gallons total for two coats of semi-transparent stain. Rough, dry, or weathered wood needs more.

## The formula for deck stain gallons

Measure the deck, pick a coverage rate for your wood, then work out each coat on its own.

**Gallons to buy = (deck area in sq ft / first coat coverage) + (deck area in sq ft / second coat coverage), for two-coat products. For a one-coat product, use the first part only. Then round up to whole gallons.**

The split matters. Behr Premium Semi-Transparent Stain and Sealer lists 250 to 300 sq ft per gallon for the first coat and 500 to 600 sq ft per gallon for the second, and it calls for two thin coats. The second coat goes about twice as far because the first coat has filled the pores of the wood.

Other labels show how wide the range can be:

| Product and wood | Coverage per gallon |
| --- | --- |
| Cabot semi-transparent, smooth wood | 250 to 350 sq ft |
| Cabot semi-transparent, rough wood | 100 to 200 sq ft |
| Thompson's WaterSeal Advanced, smooth wood | 225 sq ft |
| Thompson's WaterSeal Advanced, rough sawn wood | 125 sq ft |
| Sherwin-Williams SuperDeck waterborne semi-transparent | 100 to 350 sq ft |

Angi gives a broad cross-check of 150 to 300 sq ft per gallon, based on age, condition, and porosity. Use the low end of your label range for old or rough boards. Our calculator uses the same split, with size, wood condition, and coats as inputs.

## Worked example: a 16 x 20 ft deck, two coats

Say your deck is 16 x 20 ft (4.9 x 6.1 m), the boards are smooth and in fair shape, and you picked a two-coat semi-transparent stain. This example covers the floor only. Railings and steps are extra, covered below.

Step 1, find the area. 16 ft x 20 ft = 320 sq ft.

Step 2, first coat at the low end of the Behr rate, 250 sq ft per gallon. 320 / 250 = 1.28 gallons.

Step 3, second coat at the low end of the second coat rate, 500 sq ft per gallon. 320 / 500 = 0.64 gallons.

Step 4, add the coats. 1.28 + 0.64 = 1.92 gallons.

Step 5, round up like a buyer. You cannot buy 1.92 gallons, so buy 2 gallons.

Check it a second way: 1.28 plus 0.64 adds back to 1.92 gallons. The bit left over is touch-up stock for worn steps.

For cost, Angi's 2026 figures put semi-transparent stain at $30 to $50 per gallon, and many DIY stains with built-in sealant at about $40 per gallon. Two gallons comes to $60 to $100 for stain alone. Solid stain runs $35 to $55 per gallon on the same Angi table, so a solid color would cost $70 to $110 for stain.

## How to measure your deck

Measure length and width in feet and multiply for square feet. For an L-shaped deck, split it into two rectangles, work out each one, and add them. Our [square footage calculator](/blog/square-footage-calculator/) handles odd shapes if your deck wraps a corner or a pool.

Do not stop at the floor. For steps, measure each tread and riser and add that area in. For railings, measure length times height as one rough block, and count both faces if you stain both sides. A long railing can add 40 to 80 sq ft, enough to push a small deck into one more gallon.

Walk the deck before you buy. Replace rotten or split boards first, because new boards drink stain at a different rate than old ones. Our [deck board calculator](/blog/deck-board-calculator/) helps you count replacement boards and screws.

## What changes the gallons you need?

Wood condition is the big one. Smooth, sound boards sit near the top of a label range. Rough sawn, cracked, or gray boards sit near the bottom. Cabot puts that gap at 250 to 350 sq ft per gallon on smooth wood and 100 to 200 sq ft on rough wood for the same stain. That is close to twice the stain for rough wood.

Product type matters too. Some stains are one-coat products, such as the Cabot semi-transparent above. Thompson's WaterSeal waterproofing stains list 150 to 400 sq ft per gallon and are sold as one coat. Others, such as the Behr semi-transparent, require two thin coats. Read the coats line on your can and match the math to it.

Spraying uses more stain than a pad or brush. Wind, overspray, and board gaps all come out of the same can. Spray in small sections and back-brush at once, as the Behr label directs.

The same math works for a fence, counted on the faces you will stain. For a fence job, use our [fence stain calculator](/blog/fence-stain-calculator/), the fence mode of this tool.

## Mistakes that leave you short or overbuying

The most common error is using paint coverage for stain. Wall paint often covers 350 to 400 sq ft per gallon, but stain soaks in instead of sitting on top, so most deck stains cover less on the first coat.

The second error is pricing both coats at the first coat rate. That overbuys, because the second coat spreads about twice as far. The opposite error is buying one gallon for a two-coat job because the floor area fits inside the first coat rate alone.

Do not stain new pressure-treated wood too soon. Cabot gives a plain test: sprinkle water on the boards. If it soaks in fast, the wood can take stain. If it beads up, wait or sand lightly and test again.

Last, if your math lands close to a whole number, buy the extra gallon unopened. Most stores take back an unopened can, and a mid-job run can show as lap marks.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much stain do I need for a 12 x 16 ft deck?
The floor is 192 sq ft. At 250 sq ft per gallon for a first coat you need 0.77 gallons, and at 500 sq ft per gallon for a second coat you need 0.38 gallons, for 1.15 gallons total. Buy 1 gallon plus 1 quart, or 2 gallons if your color comes in gallons only.

### How many gallons of stain for a 500 sq ft deck?
For smooth wood and two coats, plan on 500 / 250 = 2 gallons for the first coat and 500 / 500 = 1 gallon for the second, or 3 gallons total. For rough wood at 150 sq ft per gallon on the first coat, plan on about 4 to 5 gallons total and check your label.

### Do I need one coat or two coats of deck stain?
It depends on the can, not on habit. Behr semi-transparent stain calls for two thin coats, while Cabot semi-transparent stain and Thompson's WaterSeal waterproofing stains are sold as one-coat products. A second coat over a one-coat penetrating stain can stay tacky or peel.

### How much does a gallon of deck stain cost in 2026?
Angi's 2026 data puts semi-transparent stain at $30 to $50 per gallon and solid stain at $35 to $55 per gallon. Across all stain types Angi lists $20 to $120 per gallon, with oil-based and semi-solid products at the high end.

### How much stain do I need for deck railings and steps?
Measure them as area, just like the floor. Add tread and riser area for steps, and length times height for each railing face, then run that area through the same coverage rate. On many decks, railings and steps add 15 to 30 percent to the floor area.
